common_name: Chuck Begnaud Louisiana Iris (Lavender Ruffled Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall into a sunny, constantly wet, slightly acidic bed so the clump establishes before its early-midseason bloom.

directions: Chuck Begnaud bears ruffled, rich lavender flowers edged in white, with a gold ray signal rimmed white on the falls and dark lavender style arms that lighten toward the tip. It was registered by hybridizer Dorman Haymon and named in memory of a longtime Society for Louisiana Irises member. It blooms in the early midseason window, somewhat ahead of many later Louisiana iris cultivars. Grow it in full sun in soil or shallow water that never dries out, dividing congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Jacaranda Lad Louisiana Iris (Blue Veined Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall into a sunny, constantly wet bed or pond margin ahead of its tall midseason bloom stalks.

directions: Jacaranda Lad opens soft jacaranda-blue flowers veined in a darker blue, with falls marked by a bright lime-green steeple signal and jacaranda-blue style arms edged in cream. Bred by Australian hybridizer Heather Pryor from a cross of 'Sea Wisp' and 'Spanish Ballet', it reaches a tall 36 to 40 inches and blooms in midseason on well-branched stalks. It has gone on to parent further Louisiana iris cultivars, a sign of its garden-worthy color and form. Grow in full sun in soil or shallow water that stays reliably wet, and divide crowded clumps every few years after bloom.
